notes:
CS201 notes - Kevin

TOPIC 1: Linked lists vs arrays
- array = contiguous mem, O(1) random access, insert/delete in middle O(n) bc shifting
- dyn array (ArrayList) doubles when full -> amortized O(1) append. resize itself O(n) tho
- singly LL: node = data + next. head ptr only. insert at head O(1), search O(n)
- doubly LL: prev + next, can delete a node in O(1) if u have the ref to it. extra mem tho
- keep a tail ptr -> addLast O(1)
- common bug: losing ref to rest of list when relinking!! do new.next = cur.next FIRST, then cur.next = new
- null check on head for empty list
- when to use? lots of inserts/deletes at front = LL. need index access = array

TOPIC 2: BST
- left < node < right (for every node, not just the kids!!)
- search/insert: compare, go L or R. avg O(log n), worst O(n) if sorted input -> becomes a linked list (skewed)
- delete 3 cases:
  1) leaf -> just remove
  2) one child -> replace node w/ child
  3) two kids -> replace w/ inorder successor (min of right subtree) then delete the successor
- inorder traversal gives SORTED order (L, node, R)
- preorder = node,L,R (good for copying tree), postorder = L,R,node (deleting tree)
- height of 1 node tree = 0 (prof's convention, check hw)
- BFS/level order uses a queue, DFS ones use stack/recursion
- TODO: practice deleting from the tree on slide 14, review heap vs BST diff before quiz 3
- Q for office hrs: why does AVL need balance factor only -1,0,1?

transcript:
Okay, so, um, let's get started. Today we're gonna talk about tree traversals, and, uh, we'll tie it back to binary search trees from last week. So, can everybody see the board? Good.

So a traversal is just, um, a systematic way of visiting every node in a tree exactly once. With a list it's easy, right, you just start at the head and go. With a tree there's a choice, because each node has, like, up to two children. So we have to decide the order. And there are basically three depth-first orders, and then one breadth-first.

Let's start with inorder. Inorder is: go left, visit the node, go right. So, um, recursively, you call inorder on the left child, then you print the current node, then you call inorder on the right child. And here's the cool thing, if the tree is a binary search tree, inorder gives you the keys in sorted order. Every time. So that's, uh, that's basically a free sort, if you've built the tree. This will be on the exam, so make sure you can explain why it's sorted, not just that it is. The reason is the BST property, everything on the left is smaller, everything on the right is bigger.

Okay, preorder. Preorder is visit the node first, then left, then right. So the root always comes out first. This is useful if you wanna, um, copy a tree, or save it to a file, because when you read it back in the same order you can rebuild the same shape. And postorder is left, right, then the node. So the root comes out last. That's what you want if you're deleting a tree, because you need to free the children before you free the parent. Um, yeah.

Side note, I, uh, I was at the campus coffee place this morning and they've changed the cups again, and honestly I preferred the old ones. Anyway. Not relevant. Back to trees.

So let's do an example. Say we insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14. Root is 8. Three goes left, ten goes right, one goes left of three, six goes right of three, fourteen goes right of ten. Who wants to give me the preorder? Yeah, 8, 3, 1, 6, 10, 14. Nice. Inorder, anybody? One, three, six, eight, ten, fourteen. See, sorted. And postorder is 1, 6, 3, 14, 10, 8. Right, root last.

Now level order, that's the breadth-first one. You visit the root, then all the nodes at depth one, then depth two, and so on. So you can't just use plain recursion for that. You use a queue. You put the root in the queue, and then while the queue isn't empty, you take one out, visit it, and add its children. So that's 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14 for our tree. Um, and the depth-first ones, they use the call stack, or an explicit stack if you wanna do it iteratively.

Time complexity, everybody asks. Each node is visited once, so all of these are O(n). Space is O(h) for the recursive ones, because of the call stack, where h is the height. And that's O(n) in the worst case if the tree is skewed. For level order the queue can hold up to about half the nodes, so O(n) too.

Okay, announcements before we finish. Quiz 3 is moving. It was this Friday, October 23rd, but it's now going to be Wednesday, October 28th, because I wanna get through heaps first. Same topics, so BST operations, traversals, and heaps. Assignment 4 is still due this Friday at 11:59. Alright, so, um, for Wednesday, read the heap chapter, and try writing iterative inorder with a stack. See you then.
